text:
Unofficial English Translation

JB3398

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE
OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

QUEBEC

No.:

200-17-004014-031

DATE:

QUEBEC
,

January 13, 2005

______________________________________________________________________

JUSTICE
JEAN BOUCHARD

______________________________________________________________________

YVES
MICHAUD,
domiciled and
residing at 4765 Méridian Avenue,
Montreal
, Quebec,

H3W 2C3

Plaintiff

v.

MICHEL
BISSONNETTE,
in his
capacity as Speaker of the National Assembly of Quebec, having his office at
the Hôtel du Parlement, 1045 des Parlementaires, Room 1.30, Quebec City,
district of Quebec, G1A 1A4

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

J U D G M E N T

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

On December 13, 2000, the plaintiff Yves Michaud
delivered a speech before the
Commission des États généraux sur la situation
et l'avenir de la langue française au Québec
[Estates-General on the
Situation and Future of the French Language in Québec] (
P-1
). The
subject of this speech was the francization of immigrants.

[
2
]

On the following day, December 14, 2000, the
National Assembly unanimously adopted a motion without notice denouncing the
plaintiff’s remarks, describing them as unacceptable comments regarding ethnic
communities and the Jewish community in particular (
P-2, P-3
).

[
3
]

The plaintiff presents a motion for a
declaratory judgment asking the Court to declare that the National Assembly did
not have the power to pass this motion criticizing him, a simple citizen, for
his opinions.

[
4
]

Invoking the right of petition to the National
Assembly for the redress of grievances as set out in
section 21
of the
Charter
of human rights and freedoms
(
R.S.Q.
, c. C-12), Mr. Michaud
asks the Court to declare that the National Assembly had an obligation to rule
on his December 13, 2001 petition (
P-5.1
) or any other petition that he
might subsequently submit if the first one lapsed as the result of the dissolution
of the 36th Legislature of Quebec (
D-1
) on March 12, 2003.

THE FACTS

[
5
]

Although the plaintiff’s remedy raises primarily
questions of law, the facts deserve some attention because they will provide a
more nuanced understanding of some of the allegations in his motion and help us
respond to a number of his arguments.

[
6
]

On June 29, 2000, the government issued
Order-in-council No. 875-2000 creating the
Commission des États généraux sur
la situation et l'avenir de la langue française au Québec
[Estates-General
on the Situation and Future of the French Language in Quebec] (
D-2
).
This Commission, which was to report to the ministry responsible for the
Charter
of the French language
, and whose eleven members were appointed by the
government, was instructed to report on the trends, priorities, and resulting
consensus, and to recommend measures intended to ensure the use, status, and
quality of the French language in Québec.

[
7
]

As mentioned, the plaintiff’s remarks before the
Commission were made on December 13, 2000. They were expected. At the time, the
plaintiff was engaged in a political comeback, seeking the nomination as Parti
Québécois candidate in the riding of Mercier. In the days preceding his speech,
he had appeared on a radio program and made remarks to the effect that the
Jewish people were not the only ones in the history of humanity to have
suffered. The media reported on these remarks, which generated strong reactions
from the Jewish community and its representatives (
D-4
).

[
8
]

When he appeared before the Commission, then,
the glare of the spotlight was already on the plaintiff. The press referred to
him as a [
translation
] “star
witness” (
D-3
).

[
9
]

It is not easy to summarize a person’s remarks
or to cite only a few excerpts that may not convey his meaning when taken out
of context. Because the plaintiff’s speech was approximately fifteen pages
long, however, the Court must attempt it.

[
10
]

The speech delivered by the plaintiff discussed
the francization of immigrants as a way of achieving sovereignty for Quebec (P-1).

[
11
]

At the outset, the plaintiff affirmed that over
half of Quebec immigrants are
assimilated into the English-speaking minority, which represents 8% of the
Québec population. He went on to say:

[
translation
]

To
be or not to be assimilated? That is the question. Quebec sovereignty is
indispensable without the support, contribution and determination of a
substantial number of new Quebecers willing to journey with us and play a role
in building a society founded on social justice and freedom.

[
12
]

Moving on to the failure of the 1995 referendum,
the plaintiff criticized as follows, for example, the voting results in the
Côte St-Luc Jewish community:

[
translation
]

If
it were so [the francization of immigrants], we would not see results like the
1995 referendum results. I live on the edge of French-speaking and
English-speaking Montréal, in Côte St-Luc, where, as you can see in the
appendix to this document, there are 12 ridings, 2275 voters, not a single
"yes" vote in the 12 ridings. Not one "yes" vote, 2265
[sic] "no votes". Not even a distracted student who voted
"yes". Not even a blind or visually impaired person who made a
mistake. It's zero intolerance.

…

.
. . if immigrants, and the ones in Côte St-Luc, they're a large proportion,
understood us when we speak to them, if they understood our language, if they
understood the basic stakes for a people entitled to their own homeland, maybe
a few of them would vote "yes", whereas it was a massive
"no" vote.

[
13
]

Here is what the plaintiff said about those who
advocate tolerance:

[
translation
]

A
minority does not have to be tolerant. Tolerance is a virtue of the strongest,
of the lord, it is a virtue of a master toward his slave. Masters are tolerant
of their slaves. Tolerance is for the strongest.

[
14
]

Lastly, the plaintiff did indeed refer to the
Jewish people, but his comments were not the same as in his radio interview
beforehand:

[
translation
]

My
fellow citizens should follow the example of Canon Groulx's remarks about the
Jewish people. Canon Groulx said and invited us, and I quote "to have the
Jews' fierce will to survive, their indomitable spirit of solidarity, their
indestructible moral
fibre
". The historian then gave the example of
the Jewish people as a model that Quebecers should take to heart to affirm
their own national identity and assume, fully assume, the heritage of their
history, adding that anti-Semitism was "an un-Christian attitude and that,
spiritually, Christians are in a sense Semite". End of quote.

Canon
Groulx, who was a mentor of two (2) generations of Quebecers  and who had
a metro station named after him, which some people wanted renamed a few years
ago, no doubt to "Mordecai-Richler" station, boulevard René-Lévesque
no doubt to boulevard "Ariel Sharon", Place Jacques-Cartier probably
to Place "Galganov", and so forth. I'm being a bit satirical, I say
these things somewhat jokingly, but I think there are some who exaggerate and
push things a bit too far.

[
15
]

The reaction to plaintiff’s remarks was
immediate. The very next day, leader of the official opposition Jean Charest
put a question to Premier Lucien Bouchard on the floor of the National
Assembly, asking him whether he approved of the plaintiff’s remarks and whether
he would still agree to his nomination as candidate for the Parti Québécois in
the Mercier riding. Mr. Bouchard replied that he was in total disagreement with
the plaintiff’s remarks, which he deplored and condemned. As for the nomination
in the riding of Mercier, Mr. Bouchard would let the appropriate party
authorities decide that question (
P-3
).

[
16
]

Informed that the text of a joint motion by a
Liberal MLA and a Parti Québécois MLA was circulating, Mr. Bouchard also
informed the National Assembly that he supported it entirely, as would all
members of the government when it was presented. This occurred a few moments
later, without debate, [
translation
]
“given that the text speaks for itself and is introduced by members on both
sides of the National Assembly
,
”

explained the leader of the
official opposition (
P-3
).

[
17
]

The motion without notice reads as follows (
P-2
):

[
translation
]

Motions without notice

By consent of the Assembly to set
aside section 185 of the Rules, Mr. Bergman (D'Arcy-McGee) and Mr. Boulerice
(Sainte-Marie–Saint-Jacques) jointly move:

That the National Assembly
uncompromisingly, unequivocally and unanimously denounces the unacceptable
remarks about ethnic communities and, in particular, the Jewish community, made
by Yves Michaud in Montréal, on December 13, 2000, at the Estates-General
hearings on the French language.

The motion is put to a vote; a vote
by roll call is required.

The
motion is passed by the following vote:

Yea:

109
Nay:
0
Abstaining:
0

[
18
]

The plaintiff, informed of it at the last minute
by a journalist, states that he watched it on television, appalled, as the motion
was presented. Since then, he states, not a day has passed without his feeling
the injury inflicted by those [
translation
]
“tin solders,” muzzled and trapped by parliamentary procedure, rising on cue to
heap shame and dishonour upon him (
P-5
)
.

[
19
]

It is not my intent to trivialize what the
plaintiff may have felt when this motion was brought. Beyond what he has
stated, however, it is important to point out that he quickly received a good
deal of support for his cause, including approximately thirty public figures,
led by former Premier Jacques Parizeau, who signed an open letter that claimed
that the motion of censure by the National Assembly was a serious impingement
on rights and freedoms and a flagrant act of injustice (
D-6
). This was December 18, 2000.
[1]

[
20
]

In fact, the general uproar created by this
matter continued until January 11, 2001, both within the ranks of sovereignists
and among the general public, with those who supported the plaintiff facing off
against those who approved of the treatment he received from the elected
officials.

[
21
]

On January 11, 2001, Lucien Bouchard’s
announcement of his withdrawal from politics diverted media attention and
closed the first chapter of what it is now commonly called the “Michaud
Affair.” Without naming the plaintiff, Mr. Bouchard wrote: [
translation
] “I still don’t understand
how the linguistic debate came to shift to a comparative quantification of the
sufferings of the Jewish people and the so-called intolerance showed by
Quebecers who did not vote for Quebec sovereignty.” (
D‑6
).

[
22
]

The next relevant occurrence took place on May 3, 2001. On that date, the plaintiff filed a
petition at the National Assembly in which he [
translation
] “demands to be heard by the Commission of the
National Assembly so that he may enlighten its members on the motion concerning
him voted on December 14, 2000.”

(
P-4
).

[
23
]

His petition was formally accepted. Within the
next few days, the plaintiff also submitted a brief in the event he would be
heard. In his brief, he urged the National Assembly to revise its rules to
ensure that the freedom of thought and expression of a citizen would never
again be subject to censure (
P-5
).

[
24
]

Although an excerpt of the petition was
submitted on May 3, 2001, the
National Assembly never actually entered it on the order paper for debate. The
brief the plaintiff submitted has been archived for reference, however, and is
included in the documents of the National Assembly that are available for
consultation. Its content was also circulated in the print media (
D-7
).

[
25
]

On December 13, 2001, the plaintiff filed a
second petition at the National Assembly seeking redress for the injustice
resulting from the passage of the motion denouncing his remarks regarding
ethnic communities (
P-5.1
). In this petition, the plaintiff sought one of
the following remedies:

[
translation
]

That the National Assembly
acknowledge that the vote on its motion of December 14, 2000 concerning the
remarks made by Yves Michaud was not preceded by the tabling of the transcript
of the remarks or by their full recitation in a plenary session and that,
accordingly, the MNAs could not judge the acceptability of the remarks before
supporting the motion; or

That the National Assembly declare
that, as an institution, it does not have the authority or power to express an
opinion endorsing or reproving remarks made by a citizen who is not one of its
Members.

[
26
]

That same day, in accordance with the rules then
in force (
Standing Orders of the National Assembly (Standing Orders),
s.
64.1),

the director of the Secretariat of the Assembly sent the House
Leader a copy of this petition. The government had sixty days after the filing
of the petition to respond in writing, unless the Assembly was not in session,
in which case its response had to be presented within three days of the
resumption of parliamentary proceedings (
P-5.3
).

[
27
]

On March 12, 2002, when the Assembly resumed
work after its adjournment on December 21, 2001 (
Standing

Orders
,
s. 19), the Minister responsible for Parliamentary Reform wrote to the
plaintiff and informed him of his intention to bring a proposal before the
National Assembly Commission that a new rule be adopted regarding motions to
censure a person who is not a member (
P-6
).

[
28
]

At the time, the plaintiff appeared to be
satisfied with this letter, saying [
translation
]
“This brings a sad episode of parliamentary history to an end” (
D-8
).

[
29
]

Unfortunately for him, however, the National
Assembly Commission did not move its proceedings forward (
P-7
) before
the dissolution of the 36th legislature on March 12, 2003 (
D-1
). Consequently,
under section 47 of the
Standing Orders,
the proposal to adopt a rule to
govern motions of censure lapsed. The plaintiff therefore instituted the
present proceeding.

CLAIMS OF THE PARTIES

[
30
]

The plaintiff maintains that the December 14,
2000 motion was beyond the powers of the National Assembly. He acknowledges the
inherent privilege of the National Assembly to govern its internal affairs
without outside interference and the privilege enshrining the freedom of speech
of members. He maintains, however, that these privileges cannot be invoked in
the present case because the National Assembly was neither fulfilling its
legislative function nor exercising its power of supervision over the
executive.

[
31
]

With respect to the petition filed at the
National Assembly on December 13, 2001 or any other petition that he might
file, the plaintiff argues that
section 21
of the
Charter of human rights
and freedoms

requires the National Assembly to review a grievance submitted
by petition on its merits and to issue a ruling either accepting or refusing
the request to redress the said grievance.

[
32
]

The defendant, in his capacity as Speaker of the
National Assembly, submits that the parliamentary privileges invoked cannot be
limited to cases where members study a bill or supervise government action. In
the view of the defendant, they apply to the present case and the Court
therefore has no jurisdiction to review the exercise of such privileges.

[
33
]

In response to the plaintiff’s claim that
section
21
of the
Charter
imposes an obligation on the National Assembly to rule
on a petition, the defendant maintains that this provision merely codifies
earlier law and the Assembly alone may approve the right of any person to file
a petition.

THE LAW

[
34
]

The starting point of any analysis of whether a
legislative assembly may lawfully claim a parliamentary privilege and thereby
be exempted from judicial review is the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada
in
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of
Assembly)
,

1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319.

[
35
]

In that judgment, set against the background of
the decision by the House of Assembly of Nova Scotia to prohibit the media from
filming its debates, a majority of the members of the Court found that the
privileges of provincial legislative assemblies have a constitutional status
that shelters them from review under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
, because one part of the Constitution cannot be abrogated by
another (at 390).

[
36
]

This initial finding should not be interpreted
as exempting all actions performed by a legislative assembly from judicial
review, however. It applies only to those actions that are within the territory
of parliamentary privilege (at 370‑371):

Nor does a purposive interpretation of
s. 32(1) lead to the conclusion that the
Charter
does not apply to
a legislative assembly, in my view. It is argued that the history of
curial deference to legislative bodies means that the
Charter
can never
apply to them. The argument, with respect, is cast too broadly.
The
tradition of curial deference does not extend to everything a legislative
assembly might do, but is firmly attached to certain specific activities of
legislative assemblies, i.e.,

the so‑called privileges of such
bodies
. It follows that the tradition of curial deference to
legislative bodies does not support a blanket rule that the
Charter

cannot apply to any of the actions of a legislative assembly

Without deciding that the
legislative assembly is a government actor for all purposes, suffice it to say
that as a public body it might be capable of impinging on individual freedoms
in
areas not protected by privilege
. …

[
37
]

What, then, constitutes a parliamentary
privilege and what are they specifically?

[
38
]

To answer this question, we must refer to the
preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, which states that our
constitution is similar in principle to that of the United
Kingdom. It is a parliamentary government that grants
certain privileges to Parliament and its members, and as a result, the National
Assembly and its members enjoy similar privileges which, it should be recalled,
also enjoy constitutional status (at 378).

[
39
]

These privileges, which denote the legal
exemption from some duty or liability to which other persons are subject (at
378), are not unlimited. The status of privilege is conferred only upon what is

necessary
for the proper functioning of the legislative body that claims
them (at 381).

[
40
]

In this respect, certain specific privileges are
recognized, which means that there is no requirement to demonstrate their necessity.
They are (at 385):

(a) freedom of speech, including
immunity from civil proceedings with respect to any matter arising from the
carrying out of the duties of a member of the House of Assembly;

(b) exclusive control over their
own proceedings;

(c) ejection of strangers from the
House and its precincts; and

(d) control of publication of
debates and proceedings in the House.

[
41
]

A
mong the privileges mentioned above, the
National Assembly invokes the freedom of speech of its members and the
exclusive control by the National Assembly over its own proceedings to oppose
the remedy sought by the plaintiff. The question as to the role of the Court in
such circumstances therefore arises.

[
42
]

Again, the Supreme Court in
New Brunswick
Broadcasting Co.
provides the analytical model to answer this question: the
Court may verify the existence and scope of a privilege, but not its exercise.
McLachlin J., for the majority, stated the following on this subject:

The test of necessity is not
applied as a standard for judging the content of a claimed privilege, but for
the purpose of determining the necessary sphere of exclusive or absolute
"parliamentary" or "legislative" jurisdiction.
If a
matter falls within this necessary sphere of matters without which the dignity
and efficiency of the House cannot be upheld, courts will not inquire into
questions concerning such privilege. All such questions will instead fall to
the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislative body.
(at 383)

… Were the courts to examine the
content of particular exercises of valid privilege, and hold some of these
exercises invalid, they would trump the exclusive jurisdiction of the
legislative body, after having admitted that the privilege in issue falls
within the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislative body.
The only area for
court review is at the initial jurisdictional level: is the privilege claimed
one of those privileges necessary to the capacity of the legislature to
function?
A particular exercise of a necessary privilege cannot then be
reviewed, unless the deference and the conclusion reached at the initial stage
be rendered nugatory.

In summary, it seems clear that,
from an historical perspective, Canadian legislative bodies possess such
inherent privileges as may be necessary to their proper functioning. These
privileges are part of the fundamental law of our land, and hence are
constitutional
. The courts may determine if the privilege claimed is
necessary to the capacity of the legislature to function, but have no power to
review the rightness or wrongness of a particular decision made pursuant to the
privilege
. (at 384-385)

[
43
]

It is with these considerations in mind that the
Court shall now address the arguments of the parties.

ANALYSIS

Validity of the motion adopted by the
National Assembly on December 14, 2000

[
44
]

The plaintiff recognizes the existence of the
two privileges claimed in this case by the National Assembly, namely, the
freedom of speech of its members and the right of the assembly to regulate its
internal affairs without outside interference. In addition, the Supreme Court
not only recognizes these privileges, but affirms that their necessity is
obvious (at 385-386).

[
45
]

The issue that the Court must decide, therefore,
is not whether these privileges exist but what their scope is.

[
46
]

In this respect, the plaintiff maintains in his
first submission that, to be claimed, the privilege must fall under one of the
following functions of the National Assembly:

▪

the legislative function;

▪

the supervision of executive power.

[
47
]

The plaintiff argues that when the National
Assembly passed the motion concerning him on December 14, 2000, it was not exercising
either of these functions and therefore could not legally invoke these two
privileges without diverting them from their intended purpose.

[
48
]

The plaintiff appears before the Court as a
simple citizen, a victim of the violation of his right not to be interfered
with because of his opinions. According to the plaintiff, the National Assembly
clearly exceeded its powers by censuring him for his remarks and it therefore
should not be able to invoke its parliamentary privileges.

[
49
]

This Court is not persuaded that the National
Assembly is prohibited from censuring remarks that its members collectively
deem to be unacceptable, due to the central position that this body occupies in
our system of government. There is no question that its primary mission is to
study and pass bills and to supervise the government’s activity. The Court does
not believe, however, that the Assembly’s powers are limited to that.

[
50
]

Even an inattentive observer of the
parliamentary scene could not fail to notice the diversity of subjects that are
discussed during sessions of the National Assembly, in addition to the
introduction of bills or the review of acts of the government (
Standing
Orders,
ss. 51-54). If members of the National Assembly could be challenged
outside this limited framework without being able to invoke their privileges,
the very function of this tribune, a site for the confrontation of diverse
ideas and the embodiment of [
translation
]
“a microcosm of Québec society in all its complexity and variety
,”
would
be jeopardized (Jean-Noël Lavoie
,

Organisation et fonctionnement de
l’Assemblée Nationale,
Quebec, 1976 at 5).

[
51
]

This first conclusion disposes of the
defendant
’s argument that the motion of
December 14, 2000 is
ultra

vires
because the National Assembly
exceeded its jurisdiction. As the Supreme Court decided in
New Brunswick
Broadcasting Co.
,
once the Court recognizes the privilege claimed and its
application, as is the case here, its consideration of the matter must cease
and it cannot review the exercise of the privilege.

[
52
]

The Court nevertheless considers it appropriate
to put certain facts into context.

[
53
]

First, it is not accurate for the plaintiff to
present himself as a simple citizen, an individual.

[
54
]

He has been the manager and editor-in-chief of
three newspapers, a member of the National Assembly from 1966 to 1970, an
advisor to the Premier, the Delegate General of Quebec in France, and the
Chairman of the Palais des congrès de Montréal. What is more, when he made the
comments that gave rise to the censure, he was attempting a political comeback
by seeking the Parti Québécois nomination in the riding of Mercier.

[
55
]

This is the first qualification the Court feels
it should make, and it believes that lends a particular colour to the matter at
hand.

[
56
]

There are others.

[
57
]

The plaintiff’s remarks were made before the
Commission of the Estates-General on the Situation and Future of the French
Language in Quebec, which was
created by the government (
supra
at

para. 6). That being so, how
can the plaintiff maintain that the motion subsequently adopted by the National
Assembly went beyond its function of supervising the acts of the Government,
its departments, and its agencies (
Act respecting the National Assembly,
R.S.Q
.

ch
. A-
23.1, s. 4)? While it is true that the plaintiff was not a
member of the commission, he did testify before it and made controversial
political remarks, touching on issues that are very sensitive in Quebec public opinion. The Commission’s
mandate was to report to the ministry responsible for the
Charter of the
French language,
which would in turn make its report to the government.

[
58
]

In the opinion of the Court, the reaction of the
National Assembly to these remarks falls within its function of supervising
government activity. In addition, it was the expression of the freedom of
speech of the members of the Assembly, who voted by roll call. Therefore, a
judge may not question the Assembly; doing so would very quickly drag the judge
into the heart of a political debate, which is not appropriate to the judicial
role.

[
59
]

Therefore, the privileges of freedom of speech
of the members and the right of the National Assembly to regulate its internal
affairs without outside interference are applicable in the present case.
Consequently, the Court does not have the authority to consider the merits of
the motion and the exercise of the privileges.

Obligation
of the National Assembly to rule on the petition of
December 13, 2001

[
60
]

The petition that the plaintiff presented to the
National Assembly is grounded on
section 21
of the
Charter of human rights
and freedoms
.
This provision is found in Chapter II of the
Charter
entitled
POLITICAL RIGHTS and reads as follows:

21. Every person has a right of
petition to the National Assembly for the redress of grievances
.

[
61
]

The plaintiff submits that this provision, which
is quasi-constitutional in nature and takes precedence over other laws pursuant
to
section 52
of the
Charter
, not only obliges the National Assembly to
rule on his petition but also obliges the Court to ensure the protection of
this right if it is violated by the Assembly.

[
62
]

In response to this argument, it should be
pointed out that the right of a citizen to petition the National Assembly for
the redress of a grievance existed long before it was entrenched in the
Charter

in 1975:

All authorities agree that the
right of petitioning parliament for redress of grievances is acknowledged as a
fundamental principle of the constitution. It has been uninterruptedly exercised
from very early times and has had a profound effect in determining the main
forms of parliamentary procedure. (Speaker Gaspard Fauteux,
Debates
,
June 18, 1947, at 4278-9, in Robert Marleau & Camille Montpetit,
House
of Commons Procedure and Practice
(Ottawa: House of Commons,
Chenelière/McGraw-Hill–Montreal/Toronto) at 923).

[
63
]

The exercise of this time-honoured right,
however, has always been subject to or circumscribed by the privileges of the
Assembly.

[
64
]

The question, therefore, is whether the
codification of this right in the
Charter
changed it so profoundly that
a judge now has the authority to give orders to the National Assembly.

[
65
]

The interpreter of a
Charter
right should
to adopt a broad and liberal approach that permits the full expansion of that
right. On the other hand, the interpreter must not lose sight of the context
surrounding its adoption. This was noted by McIntyre J. in
Reference re Public Service Employee Relations
Act (Alta.)
,
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 313

at 394
:

It follows that while a liberal and not overly legalistic approach
should be taken to constitutional interpretation, the
Charter
should not
be regarded as an empty vessel to be filled with whatever meaning we might wish
from time to time. The interpretation of the
Charter
, as of all constitutional
documents, is constrained by the language, structure, and history of the
constitutional text, by constitutional tradition, and by the history,
traditions, and underlying philosophies of our society.

[
66
]

In
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co.
,

supra
,
McLachlin J. also affirms that the advent of the Charters did not abrogate or
eliminate the privileges recognized as necessary to the functioning of
legislative assemblies, which would be possible only in the presence of clear
language to that effect (at 372):

I cannot, however, follow my
colleague Cory J. in concluding that “the
Charter
should apply to the actions
of the legislative assembly” (p. 401) if he means by this that the
Charter

should apply to all of the actions of the legislative assembly.
Absent specific

Charter
language to the contrary, the long history of curial deference
to the independence of the legislative body, and to the rights necessary to the
functioning of that body,
cannot be lightly set aside, even conceding that
our notions of what is permitted to government actors have been significantly
altered by the enactment and entrenchment of the
Charter
. The legal
reason why curial deference to the action of the House of Assembly here in
issue should be preserved is set out below.

[
67
]

Applied to the present case, these directives
from the Supreme Court lead the Court to conclude that
section 21
of the
Charter

does not have the scope the plaintiff claims it does.

[
68
]

First, the terms used by the legislator must be
considered. In reality, it is the right of any person to
petition
the
National Assembly that is guaranteed by
section 21
of the
Charter
. The
use of this word, far from being neutral, reveals the exact nature of this
political remedy and urges the Court to show deference to the independence of
the National Assembly and the privileges necessary to its operation.

[
69
]

Traditionally, the Assembly has the right to
exclude strangers from its premises, which are reserved for elected officials.
In Canada, legislative
assemblies are not accessible to the public by law (
New Brunswick
Broadcasting Co.
, supra
at 386-388). The right to petition must therefore
be understood in this context as neither more nor less than the right of any
ordinary citizen to enter or penetrate (in the figurative sense) the National
Assembly.

[
70
]

Moreover, the fact that the legislators specify
in
section 21
of the
Charter
that this right is to be exercised “to
redress grievances” does not change its nature and create an obligation for the
Assembly. Whenever and wherever this right to petition has existed, it has been
defined as a petition to an authority for “the redress of some wrong”:

Raymond
Guillien & and Jean Vincent,
Lexique des termes juridiques
, 13
th

ed. (Dalloz, 2001):

[
translation
]

Petition (Dr. Const)
Application for review that may be submitted, in written form,
before parliamentary assemblies to denounce an administrative abuse, recommend
a legislative amendment, etc. Procedure used
infrequently today.

Joseph R. Nolan
& Jacqueline M. Nolan-Haley,
Black's Law Dictionary
, 6
th

ed. (The Publisher's Editorial Staff, 1990):

Petition.
A written address, embodying an application or prayer from the
person or persons preferring it, to the power, body, or person to whom it is
presented, for the exercise of his or their authority
in the redress of some
wrong,
or the grant of some favor, privilege, or license. A formal written
request addressed to some governmental authority. The right of the people to
petition for redress of grievances is guaranteed by the First Amendment, U.S.
Constitution.”

John A. Yogis,

Canadian Law Dictionary,
2d ed. (Barron's Educational Series, Inc.)

PETITION
A prayer (formal request) from a person or group to a power or
person for the exercise of his authority in the redress of some wrong. In old
English law, a petition was addressed to the King and later to the Chancellor
in a situation where a case was beyond the ordinary writ system. In present
day, a divorce proceeding is started by petitioning the court.

Robert Marleau
& Camille Montpetit
, House of Commons Procedure and Practice
(Ottawa: House of Commons
,
Chenelière/McGraw-Hill–Montreal-Toronto):

Simply defined, a petition is a
formal request to an authority for redress of a grievance. Public petitions,
addressed to the House of Commons and presented to the House by its Members,
constitute one of the most direct means of communication between the people and
Parliament. Certainly, it is among the most ancient; the act of petitioning has
been described as “the oldest of parliamentary forms, the fertile seed of all
proceedings of the House of Commons”.

[
71
]

Absent “specific
Charter
language to the
contrary” of
section 21
that would allow for the inference that the legislator
intended to violate the right of the Assembly to supervise its debates, the
said section being silent with respect to how to submit a petition before the
National Assembly and the follow-up to be given to such a request, the Court
finds that the handling of a petition falls under the National Assembly’s
inherent privilege to have control over its internal procedures. Consequently,
a judge may not examine an alleged failure to follow up on a petition.

[
72
]

Authors Brun and Tremblay come to the same
conclusion (Henri Brun & Guy Tremblay
, Droit constitutionnel,
4
th

ed.,

(Cowansville, Qc.:

Yvon Blais) at 334, 335 and 912):

[
translation
]

Thus, the courts will not agree to
give orders to legislative assemblies, either directly or indirectly, because
they are masters of their own procedures…. Likewise, section 21 of the
Charter
of human rights and freedoms
, R.S.Q., c. C-12, which sets out the right of
every person to petition the National Assembly, may be sanctioned only by the
Assembly itself: …

What we have seen in this respect
regarding the
Canadian Charter
(in I.B.) also applies to the
Quebec

Charter.
Therefore, for example,
the courts are prohibited from ensuring the sanction of
section 21
of the
Charter
,
which gives every person the right to petition the National Assembly.

[
73
]

Finally, a review of parliamentary debates on
the bill that led to the adoption of the
Charter of human rights and
freedoms
reveals that the right to petition, at the time set out in
section
20
, was not even discussed (
Journal des débats
, June 25, 1975, B-5048).
In the opinion of the Court, this makes it unlikely that the National Assembly
waived its privilege of controlling its internal proceedings with respect to
the follow-up of petitions out of general indifference.

[
74
]

Therefore, the court does not grant the remedy
sought by the plaintiff and does not declare that the National Assembly was
required to rule on his December 13, 2001 petition.

CONCLUSION

[
75
]

In the view of the Court, the privileges claimed
by the National Assembly, namely, the freedom of speech of its members and the
right of the Assembly to regulate its internal proceedings without outside
interference, are not limited to cases where the Assembly exercises its
legislative function or its function of supervising executive power.

[
76
]

In the alternative, even if these privileges are
limited to such matters, it is the Court’s opinion that the National Assembly
adopted the December 14, 2000 motion in the exercise of its power of
supervision over acts of the government, the remarks of the plaintiff having
been made before the Commission of the Estates-General on the Situation and
Future of the French language in Quebec, a governmental body, at a time when
the plaintiff was attempting a political comeback.

[
77
]

Finally, section 21 of the
Charter of human
rights and freedoms

is not new law, and despite its quasi-constitutional
status, it does not interfere with the right of the National Assembly to have
exclusive control over the conduct of its proceedings and the development of
its rules of procedure.

[
78
]

Given the importance and seriousness of the
questions raised, the motion of the plaintiff is dismissed, with each party
paying its own costs.

[
79
]

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
80
]

DISMISSES
the
motion of the plaintiff;

[
81
]

WITHOUT COSTS.
